topic: Déjà vu: prevalence, age, layout familiarity, memory checking, epilepsy link
hook: Déjà vu is your brain checking itself

slides.title: Almost everyone gets it
slides.body: About two in three people say they've had déjà vu at least once. It's one of the most common odd feelings.
slides.image_prompt: A long empty hallway of identical doors fading into soft fog, one door slightly glowing, eerie calm mood

slides.title: It fades with age
slides.body: It's most frequent in teens and young adults, then shows up less and less as we get older.
slides.image_prompt: An antique clock and a stack of faded photo frames without faces on a wooden table, warm dim light

slides.title: A layout you forgot
slides.body: Lab studies show it can appear when a new place has the same layout as one you've seen but can't recall.
slides.image_prompt: Two nearly identical empty rooms side by side with the same furniture layout, one in color, one in faded grey

slides.title: Your brain fact-checking
slides.body: One leading theory: your brain's memory checker spots a false 'I've seen this' signal and flags it.
slides.image_prompt: A glowing brain model with a small magnifying glass hovering over it, dark background, soft blue light

slides.title: A seizure warning sign
slides.body: In temporal lobe epilepsy, déjà vu can come just before a seizure. That helped scientists trace where it starts.
slides.image_prompt: A translucent brain model with one side lobe glowing amber, surrounded by darkness and faint electrical sparks

caption:
That eerie feeling of 'I've lived this before' happens to about two in three people. It's most common in your teens and twenties and fades with age.

One lab finding: déjà vu can appear when a new room shares the layout of a place you've forgotten. Your brain senses the match but can't find the memory. Sources: Brown (2003, Psychological Bulletin) and Cleary et al. (2012).

Follow for one fact your brain won't believe, daily. Tomorrow: why time speeds up as you get older.
